lesson.title: What It Really Means to Solve an Equation
lesson.summary: Solving an equation means finding every value of the variable that makes both sides equal, and every valid solving move is really just an operation applied equally to both sides to keep that balance.
lesson.body:
An equation is a statement that two expressions are equal, connected by an equals sign. Solving an equation means finding the value or values of the variable that make that statement true. The core idea underneath every solving technique is balance: an equation behaves like a balanced scale, and whatever operation is done to one side must be done to the other side as well, or the scale, and the equality, is destroyed.

This builds directly on the idea of an equation itself: two expressions joined by an equals sign, each side capable of being evaluated once a value is substituted for the variable. A value is called a solution when substituting it into the equation makes the left side and the right side come out equal. Not every number you might try is a solution; testing a candidate value and checking whether both sides match is exactly how a proposed answer gets verified, which is why checking a solution by substitution, as used throughout this topic, is not an optional extra step but part of what solving means.

This balance idea is why solving techniques work at all. If x + 4 = 9, subtracting 4 from the left side isolates x, but subtracting 4 only from the left and not the right would break the equality. Subtracting 4 from both sides gives x + 4 - 4 = 9 - 4, which simplifies to x = 5. The reason this is valid is that subtracting the same number from two equal quantities always produces two more equal quantities.

Take a slightly bigger example: 3x - 7 = 14. To isolate x, first undo the subtraction of 7 by adding 7 to both sides: 3x - 7 + 7 = 14 + 7, which simplifies to 3x = 21. Then undo the multiplication by 3 by dividing both sides by 3: 3x divided by 3 = 21 divided by 3, giving x = 7. Notice that the operations were undone in reverse order from how they were built, subtraction first, then multiplication, a pattern that comes up again in every multi-step equation from here on. To check this solution, substitute x = 7 back into the original equation: 3(7) - 7 = 21 - 7 = 14, which matches the right side exactly, confirming x = 7 is correct.

Every equation-solving strategy that follows, whether it involves one step, two steps, several steps, or factoring, is built from this same foundation: apply the same operation to both sides, using inverse operations to peel away whatever is attached to the variable, one layer at a time, until the variable stands alone. Addition and subtraction undo each other, and multiplication and division undo each other, which is why those inverse pairs are the tools used to isolate a variable.

Not every equation has exactly one solution. Some, like x + 3 = x + 3, are true for every value of x, since subtracting x from both sides leaves 3 = 3, a statement that is always true regardless of x. Others, like x + 3 = x + 5, are never true for any value of x, since subtracting x from both sides leaves 3 = 5, a statement that is always false. Most of the equations encountered in early algebra, though, have exactly one solution, found by carefully applying the same operation to both sides until the variable is alone.
